Google just updated its guidance to say AI-generated content must be manually fact-checked before publishing. 
Titles, meta descriptions, schema and alt text included. 

Honestly? I read that and thought, you're only saying this now? 

Because this is what's happening on our side of the screen. Companies use AI to generate content, then decide the writer is no longer needed, or at least not full-time. Suddenly the role becomes contract or freelance, at lower pay, because AI does most of the work anyway.

No, technically, it doesn't. 
Someone still has to: 
→ know the audience and the business 
→ check every claim, stat and source 
→ fix what the tool got confidently wrong 
→ decide what the piece is actually trying to say 
→ make sure it still sounds like the brand and not like every other AI blog 

That is the job. It's skilled work, and it was never just writing. 

And when full-time roles do open up, many applications seem to go through ATS screening, which is also AI. A writer with real experience may never reach a human because the resume didn't match the right keywords. 

So we're undervalued before the work and filtered out before the interview. 

I'm not against AI. In fact, I use it, and it's useful for research, structure and first drafts. But pasting something in and typing "make it engaging" or "make it more human" isn't content drafting. Sorry mate, it just doesn't work that way. If it did, the internet wouldn't be full of content that reads the same. 

Google is now literally saying a person must review and be accountable for what gets published. So please stop treating the people who do that as replaceable, or as something you can pay less for. We're not asking for much. Just don't underestimate the writers. We're still here, and the work still needs us. 

AI can draft. Someone still has to think, check and own it. Curious how other content folks are seeing this play out.

That is why I see a Senior Forward Deployment Engineer as more than a software developer hiring checkbox. It combines product engineering, implementation, and feedback from the real environment.
For a startup tech team working on SaaS development, MVP development, or an AI-powered product, hire for the gap you have now. Choose full-time, remote, or contract support deliberately. Keep ownership close to the product.
The best hire is not the longest skills list. It is the person who can reduce the next handoff.
What would you hire for first: stack depth or end-to-end ownership?

Candidates think AI scans their CV. 
1,000+ CVs later, I can tell you: I don't need AI.

It takes me 10 seconds.
In this exact order:

1. YOUR LATEST JOB TITLE
→ Does it match the role I'm hiring for?

2. YOUR TIMELINE 
→ How long did you stay? Is there a pattern?

3. YOUR LOCATION
→ Are you here, or about to be?

4. THE FIRST 5 BULLETS OF EACH ROLE
→ Are about impact or just tasks? 

5. IS YOUR EXPERIENCE RELEVANT FOR THIS JOB? 
→ If I have to work to find the match, I move on.

I've recruited for the last 8 years and trust me, it's not as complicated as you think. 

"You need to have a CV " ATS friendly"? 
No love, you need to have a CV "recruiter friendly", because that's who actually read it. 

Technology helps us, it doesn't replace anyone. 

So here 5 simple fix: 

1. Make sure your job title is in line with your application. 
2. Month and year on every role. Short stint? One line on why (contract, relocation).
3. Your current city at the top. If you're relocating, say WHEN.
4. Lead with your biggest result, not your daily tasks.
5. Use relevant experience to match the transferable skills. 

CV doesn't have to be perfect. 
It just needs to give a reason to call you. 

Don't overcomplicate it.

AI-linked roles have accounted for more than 750,000 new jobs in the US since 2023, according to LinkedIn estimates. The largest single category added 282,000 of them. 

Published job creation data only captures new roles being posted, and it misses every existing role being repositioned around AI work inside an enterprise. 

A bank is not only hiring AI engineers. It is moving data analysts, risk modellers, and internal software teams onto agent deployment. None of that shows up as a new job created. 

Deploying AI into a large organisation turns out to require an enormous amount of technical and services work. Someone has to build the applied product, integrate it into existing systems, handle governance, and then stay involved while it actually runs. 

That is why forward deployed engineers have become a standard line item in enterprise AI contracts, and why services firms are being built specifically around deployment. 

The India relevance here is direct. This deployment layer is exactly the work Indian IT services firms have delivered for three decades, and it is the reason the AI services opportunity is likely larger than the IT services market it is supposedly replacing. 

The jobs AI creates are harder to see than the ones it displaces. They sit inside companies rather than in headlines.

AI broke my design hiring process.
I'm glad it did. 👇

The quality of design assessments I receive has never been higher.

That's become the problem.

Every take-home now arrives polished: clean layouts, tidy flows, confident rationale. And I can no longer tell a strong designer from a strong prompt.

This isn't just a design problem. If you hire developers, writers, analysts or marketers, you're facing the same question:

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲'𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝘁?

We could have banned AI from our assessments. 
We did the opposite. My team uses it every day, so testing people without it would test the wrong thing.

Which leaves a harder question: if the output no longer separates people, what does?

Nobody has a settled answer yet, and there's no widely accepted framework. 
Here's where my thinking is right now:

1. The AI disclosure is the assessment. Show me which tools you used, what you asked for, what you kept, what you threw away, and why.

2. Editing is judgement. What someone rejected tells me more than what they shipped.

3. Setup over prompting. Did you write a clear spec so the AI could work on its own, or did you steer every step? We lean towards the first: define the problem well, then let the AI run. Spec-driven, not vibe coding.

4. Improve the system, don't just use it. I want people who make the team's AI setup better for everyone.

The live walkthrough is where it all shows. 
Polished screens with thin reasoning look fine on a slide and fall apart the moment you ask "why?"

I'd rather rebuild the process than pretend the old one still works.

🤔💬 So I'm curious:

𝗛𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘀: 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗔𝗜? 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲?

You ask the model to return a simple JSON payload. It works perfectly during testing. Then production happens.

The model wraps the response in Markdown, changes an integer to a string, adds an unexpected field, or produces an invalid structure. Your Jackson ObjectMapper throws a MismatchedInputException, and an otherwise simple workflow comes to a halt.

When I first started exploring AI integrations, it was tempting to solve this entirely through Prompt Engineering:

"Return your response as a JSON object with userId and action fields."

But for critical backend operations, relying solely on prompt-based formatting is not a reliable architectural contract.

A more robust approach is Native Function Calling, also known as Tool Use.

Here is how I think about the architecture:

1. Schema Contract

Instead of asking the LLM to construct arbitrary JSON, provide a structured schema describing the available tools and their expected parameters.

This creates a much stronger contract between the model and the backend.

2. Orchestration Pause

When the LLM determines that it needs external information or an action, it does not simply generate the final response.

It produces a tool call with the required arguments.

For example, it may determine that it needs to retrieve a user's billing history before answering a question.

3. Backend Execution

The orchestration layer intercepts the tool call and maps the arguments to a strongly typed Java method.

Frameworks such as Spring AI and LangChain4j can help implement this layer.

The backend executes the actual business logic and returns the deterministic result to the LLM, which can then continue generating the final response.

4. Security Boundary

The LLM should never be treated as the authority that directly executes backend operations.

The backend should remain in control.

The orchestration layer can apply authentication, authorization, RBAC, validation, rate limiting, auditing, and other business rules before allowing a tool to execute.

This creates an important architectural boundary:

LLM → Tool Call → Backend Validation → Authorization → Business Logic → Tool Result → LLM

Building GenAI applications is therefore not just about adding intelligence to an application.

It is about designing reliable contracts, deterministic execution paths, and strong guardrails around non-deterministic components.

On day one, there was no HR function.

I had to choose what to build first.

Looking back, the order mattered as much as the work.

When I joined Code Gradients as HR Manager in September 2024, there was no structured HR function in place. I had to start building the foundation while the company was already operating and growing.

A growing software company needs everything at once.

Hiring. Contracts. Payroll. Compliance. Onboarding.

You cannot build it all at the same time.

So you choose.

My order:

Hiring workflow.
I started here because hiring directly affects how quickly a growing company can build the team it needs.

Records and compliance.
I focused on this next because the company needed reliable employee records and basic HR controls as the team grew.

Onboarding and check-ins.
I built this after the foundation because bringing people into the company properly affects how quickly they understand their role, expectations, and workplace.

What I delayed on purpose:

Building advanced HR systems before the basic HR processes were working consistently.

The rule I took from it:

Build what is already costing money first.

Build what protects the company second.

Build what improves the experience third.

Over the next 30 days I will share the systems behind this:

Hiring.
Retention.
AI in recruitment.
Policy.

I spent this quarter trying to understand why, and the sharpest answer came from Gaurav Tripathi  wrote our cover story. His argument is uncomfortable, and I think he's right!

For thirty years, IT services sold mobilisation. Finding scarce skills, clearing legal and procurement hurdles, assembling a team across geographies and time zones. That took weeks. The client paid for every hour of it.

Getting the team together was the project. Delivery came after!

That is the premium AI has compressed — not the thinking, the assembly.

Which leaves a question every services leader is now answering, deliberately or by default. If you can no longer charge for the difficulty of finding people, what are you actually selling?
Some have answered already. 

Around 80% of TCS contracts in one segment now carry outcome measures, double the level of late 2023. Cognizant and Daimler Truck split AI savings between them. HCLTech took no revenue at all in year one of its E.ON contract. (Reuters reported all three in August)

Others are holding the rate card and waiting. That is a defensible reading of an uncertain market. It is also a bet, and the renewal calendar settles it.

The October–December issue of Cerebraix Talent Tech is about that bet. Nine pieces on what replaces per-person pricing, what it costs a firm internally to make the change, and what happens to hiring once you stop selling capacity.

If you run delivery at a firm of a few hundred to a few thousand people, I'd like to know which side of that line you think you're on. Link in the first comment.

If the job has already been approved before you start building the contractor pipeline, you’re already late.

By the time many hiring managers call a recruiter:

• The project has started
• Delivery dates are fixed
• Internal teams are stretched
• Budget has been approved
• And the best available contractors may already be interviewing elsewhere

Then everyone wants speed.

But speed is usually created before the vacancy appears.

For core areas like:

Software Engineering
Cloud & Infrastructure
Data & AI
Cyber Security
Project Management & Transformation

…you should already know who is in the market.

Who is finishing a contract soon.

Who has delivered successfully before.

Who has strong references.

Who is open to the right opportunity.

And who can realistically join within the timeframe your project needs.

That is the difference between reactive recruitment and building a genuine contractor community.

When a project gets the green light, the first question shouldn’t be:

“Can you start searching?”

It should be:

“Who do we already have?”

The strongest contractor pipelines are built before demand becomes urgent.

In my view, that is where recruitment adds the most value — not simply finding somebody once the problem already exists, but helping clients prepare before it does.

Should contractor recruitment be treated more like workforce planning than vacancy filling?

When AI started reshaping banking roles, DBS had two options: replace people or redesign their jobs and reskill them for what comes next.

Here is what the bank has done:

The challenge

AI is automating many routine banking tasks. DBS slowed hiring for roles most exposed to automation and is phasing out around 4,000 contract and temporary positions over three years.

👉 Reskilled more than 11,000 employees whose roles are being significantly changed by AI
👉 Gave all 40,000 employees foundational AI training
👉 Launched a career advisory service with 100+ internal career advisors across its six core markets
👉 Paired human guidance with AI tools (iGrow and iCoach) to help employees find their strengths and plan their next move
👉 In August 2026, signed an industry-first MOU with Singapore’s Institute of Banking and Finance to build AI skills across the financial workforce

The approach

DBS’ Head of Group HR, Lee Yan Hong, describes it simply: save people, not jobs. Roles will change. The goal is to move people into work that needs human judgment and relationships.

📝 What HR leaders can take from this

Reskilling works best when it starts before roles disappear, not after.
Training alone isn’t enough. People need career conversations to see where they fit next.

Being honest about which roles are changing builds more trust than silence.
The question for every organization isn’t whether AI will change jobs. It’s whether your people will be ready when it does.

Available immediately — Senior PHP/Laravel, 8+ years, Mumbai or remote.
Before the ask, one thing that might be useful to you.

Most Laravel downtime isn't caused by bad code. It's caused by a schema change landing on top of the code version that's still running.

The fix is boring and almost nobody does it: expand → migrate → deploy → contract, as four separate steps.
◾ Expand — add the new column, nullable. Old code ignores it.
◾ Migrate — dual-write, backfill in batches. Never one giant UPDATE on a hot table.
◾ Deploy — new code reads and writes both.
◾ Contract — drop the old column. Days later. Its own deploy.
Why separate them? Rollback. If contract ships alongside expand, your only way back is restoring a backup, because you can't safely un-drop a column. If they're separate, rollback is always a code rollback.
That single decision took a deployment from "we're restoring from last night's backup" to "we rolled back and nobody noticed."

What I've shipped:
◾ Zero-downtime Nginx migrations with connection draining and health-checked traffic shifting
◾ Multi-tenant job portal end to end — candidate, employer, admin surfaces
◾ Internal Laravel package consumed by teams outside my own
◾ Monitoring and alerting dashboards — RED metrics, request IDs, alerts that catch things before customers do

The part that's unusual: I run multiple AI models locally — Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity — and orchestrate them against each other for adversarial review. I've built multi-model review councils that stress-test an architecture decision before we commit. The models reason independently, then one judges the synthesis.
Single-model review tells you what the model likes. Multi-model review tells you where the models disagree — and that disagreement is where the real risk actually lives.

Long post warning! 

I spent last week at Seattle Space Week evaluating the gaps in how we are building the space industry. 

 💫 Hannah Arendt's point about promises fits here: Action is unpredictable, so a shared future becomes reliable only when people make promises and keep them. She called them isolated islands of certainty in an ocean of uncertainty. Space Northwest's mission is that work at regional scale: powering the Pacific Northwest's space economy with bold ideas, workforce development support, and strategic partnerships. A launch site, a capital bench, and a rescue that shows up are not things one company possesses. They are agreements we still have to make and perform. 

Monday's career breakfast was open format, with participants leading the conversation. Students said they need a mentor, a project, and someone willing to say which door to knock on. Hiring managers were honest about getting in. The sector is often hardware wearing a software costume, and the space economy needs all job sectors. I perked up when legal skills came up. #SpaceNeedsLawyers 

Tuesday showed what those agreements are up against. The talent is here. The ports are here. A startling share of the satellites already in orbit were built here. A deep bench of space capital, a launch site, and an incentive sheet that wins a factory decision are not. An Earth-observation panel made the same point with a wildfire: you can own the sensor and still be late. Other panels noted that when defense pays for the first flights, commercial return follows. Retention is not a feeling. It is a partnership you build, or you watch it leave. 

On Wednesday, a robotics panel refused the usual AI confidence. A capture vehicle either takes the satellite safely or aborts. There is no undo button, and a rover should stop when it is not sure. On the factory side, human in the loop was a software phrase, not proof that a person was in control. That difference is where the liability question starts. 

Thursday's tabletop sent us to 2032, with a commercial crew and companies for propellant, communications, positioning, repair, insurance, and rescue. One scenario was a thermal fault, traced to a $37 part. No emergency delivery, because nobody had bought logistics. We called the fallback a conditional go. The vehicle could leave the surface and still miss the burn home. Repair needed drawings and a ride. Rescue existed as a prototype. Insurance was the condition of moving it. Only one contract got signed before the window closed. One promise. The rest was still ocean. 

Space Northwest and Seattle Space Week are aimed at these supporting systems. I am thankful the opportunity to help support their missions!

The 2026 Databricks Lakehouse Architecture is no longer about unifying data lakes and warehouses. That battle is won. The real frontier is unifying runtime semantics across batch, streaming, and AI inference on a single execution plane. The most advanced teams I work with are not choosing between Delta Lake and a streaming table; they are designing schemas that support both in the same pipeline, with the same governance, without duplication.

The non-obvious breakthrough is Lakebase, which turns the lakehouse into a transactional data product marketplace. The unit of value has shifted from a pipeline to a governed, shareable dataset that can be consumed by any application with zero ETL. This means the bottleneck is no longer compute or storage; it is data contract design and lineage enforcement. If your team is still treating Unity Catalog as a permissions layer rather than a deployment-time governance gate, you are leaving the primary architectural advantage on the table.

Another structural change is the automatic optimization layer embedded into the lakehouse. Databricks has published multiple papers on automatic optimizations that eliminate the need for manual tuning of file sizes, compaction, and statistics. The teams winning are the ones that lean into these declarative features and stop hand-crafting maintenance jobs. The era of the DBA who tunes partitions is ending; the era of the architect who designs for self-optimizing data is beginning.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to migrate data from one warehouse to another or tune Spark shuffle partitions. I am seeking a problem where I can design the data contract layer, enforce governance as code in Unity Catalog, and build pipelines that seamlessly span batch, streaming, and AI inference without duplication. If your team is struggling to unify real-time and batch workloads, or to govern a data product stack without creating silos, I want to hear about the specific workload patterns and compliance requirements you are facing.

What is the one architectural assumption from your current lakehouse that, if changed, would allow you to treat all data products as real-time?

Day 1 of my 8-day Digital Law series: what counts as digital law?

Here's the case. An Indian SaaS company has its engineering team in Bengaluru. Marketing launches a German landing page with prices in euros. Sales signs a pilot with a Berlin team. HR starts using a US hiring tool that stores CVs on the vendor's servers.

Then someone at the leadership meeting says: "We are an Indian company. We only need Indian law."

That line tells you where the company was born. It doesn't tell you where the humans are.

From India, digital work usually sits under three layers:

• IT Act, 2000. This is in force. It covers e-records and e-signatures (s.4, s.5) and intermediaries (s.2(1)(w)). Under s.43A, a business that is negligent with sensitive personal data owes compensation. Under s.72A, disclosing data in breach of a contract can bring a penalty of up to ₹25 lakh. CERT-In requires listed cyber incidents to be reported within six hours.
• DPDP Act, 2023. The definitions are law today. The daily duties (notice, consent, security, telling the Board about a breach, and penalties) start 18 months after the 13 Nov 2025 notification, so around May 2027. The penalty figures are maximums, not automatic fines. Start building now.
• Contracts. Customer agreements and DPAs set their own terms, and they can be stricter than the law.

Foreign law can reach you in two ways: through its statute, or through a contract that imports it. Targeting people in the EU can bring in GDPR. UK GDPR is a separate file. US state laws apply when their thresholds are met.

My ask for leaders: once a quarter, ask three questions.
1. Where do the humans sit?
2. Who decided why we hold their data?
3. Which contract already brought in someone else's law?

Day 2 tomorrow: data and roles.
